correctness.rationale: For all finite a>=2,b>=1, the bipartite metric on core A equals finite min-plus closure of two-edge minima, by walk shortening and lifting. For fixed a, a joint upper-orthant calculation shows independently Rayleigh limiting pair minima: intersections of distinct small pair events at one peripheral vertex have probability O(\(b^{-3/2}\)), negligible over b independent vertices. Continuity of graph shortest-path closure gives scaled core metric convergence. Deterministic star inequalities and removal of finite tagged vertices yield independent tagged Exp(a) leaves and independence of the two scales. verify.py checks deterministic identities by independent graph Floyd-Warshall, and exact gamma-two pair survival. No infinite limit is based only on finite experiments.

broader_coverage.reasoning: The complete-graph theorems do not dominate a regime with only a fixed number of high-degree core vertices, no core-core edges, and no peripheral-peripheral edges; there is no parameter specialization from their K_n to K_{a,b}. General shortest-path metric closure is a deterministic identity but does not cover the probabilistic joint two-scale limit. Mountford and Saliba exclude highly unbalanced deterministic bicliques because the fixed hub degrees diverge and violate the bounded degree-moment condition. Ross is a broad exact finite distribution for exponentially weighted networks but the accessible abstract does not establish the claimed asymptotic two-scale limit; this is a named residual risk.

value.rationale: The theorem identifies two simultaneously relevant but mutually distinct metric scales in a natural hub-periphery random network: an entire finite random shortest-path geometry on the fixed core at \(b^{-1/2}\) and a macroscopic exponential-star metric on finitely many peripheral tags. Their joint independence clarifies structural separation of routing fluctuations. It is not merely a normalization check or a small numerical invariant.
